title: Catabolism of Heme and Bilirubin Metabolism
objectives: Trace the pathway of heme degradation to bilirubin
Classify jaundice types and their clinical features
Explain management strategies for neonatal jaundice

heme_breakdown.title: Heme Degradation Pathway
heme_breakdown.content:
Heme Catabolism

1. Heme to Biliverdin

  • Microsomal heme oxygenase (rate-limiting)
  • Requires O2, NADPH, CYP450 reductase
  • Products: Biliverdin (green), Fe3+, CO
  • Induced by oxidative stress

2. Biliverdin to Bilirubin

  • Biliverdin reductase (NADPH-dependent)
  • Yields unconjugated bilirubin (yellow-red)

3. Hepatic Processing

  • Transport: Albumin-bound to liver
  • Uptake: Facilitated diffusion into hepatocytes
  • Conjugation: BUGT adds glucuronate (→ water-soluble)
  • Secretion: MOAT transporter into bile

4. Intestinal Fate

  • Bacterial β-glucuronidase removes glucuronides
  • Reduction to urobilinogens (colorless)
  • Excretion: Stercobilin (feces) or urobilin (urine)

hyperbilirubinemia.title: Hyperbilirubinemia Classification
hyperbilirubinemia.content:
Jaundice Pathophysiology

I. Retention Hyperbilirubinemia

  • Cause: Bilirubin overproduction (hemolysis)
  • Type: Unconjugated (lipid-soluble)
  • Risk: Kernicterus (BBB penetration)

II. Regurgitation Hyperbilirubinemia

  • Cause: Biliary obstruction/hepatic failure
  • Type: Conjugated (water-soluble)
  • Sign: Bilirubinuria (dark urine)

jaundice_types.title: Jaundice Types
jaundice_types.content:
Clinical Classification

A. Conjugated Jaundice

  • 1. Obstructive: Gallstones/pancreatic cancer (pale stool)
  • 2. Dubin-Johnson: MOAT deficiency (stress-triggered)
  • 3. Rotor Syndrome: Organic anion transport defect
  • 4. Hepatocellular: Cirrhosis/viral hepatitis

B. Unconjugated Jaundice

  • 1. Neonatal: Immature BUGT (kernicterus risk)
  • 2. BUGT Deficiencies:
    • Gilbert (30% activity)
    • Crigler-Najjar (Type I: fatal; Type II: phenobarbital-responsive)
  • 3. Hemolytic: Sickle cell/G6PD (↑urobilinogen)

management.title: Clinical Management
management.content:
Therapeutic Approaches

Neonatal Jaundice

  • Phototherapy: Converts bilirubin to soluble isomers
  • Phenobarbital: Induces BUGT (except Crigler-Najjar I)

Conjugated Jaundice

  • Obstructive: Surgical intervention
  • Dubin-Johnson/Rotor: Self-limiting (avoid triggers)

diagnostics.title: Diagnostic Markers
diagnostics.content:
Laboratory Findings

Urine/Stool Analysis

  • Obstructive: Bilirubinuria + pale stool
  • Hemolytic: ↑Urobilinogen + normal stool color
  • Hepatocellular: ↑ALT/AST + dark urine

Serum Tests

  • Total bilirubin >2mg/dL → clinical jaundice
  • Direct (conjugated) vs. indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does unconjugated bilirubin cross the BBB? +

A: Its lipid solubility allows passive diffusion into brain tissue, where it causes neurotoxicity (kernicterus) by disrupting neuronal membranes and mitochondria.

Q: How does phototherapy reduce bilirubin levels? +

A: Blue light converts unconjugated bilirubin to lumirubin and other photo-isomers that can be excreted without glucuronidation.

Q: Why does hemolysis cause increased urobilinogen but not bilirubinuria? +

A> The liver conjugates and excretes excess bilirubin as normal, but increased heme breakdown generates more urobilinogen from intestinal bacteria. Only conjugated bilirubin appears in urine, which isn't significantly elevated in pure hemolysis.
